old_title: Commonwealth Games 2026: athletics begins, plus swimming and gymnastics on day four - live
new_title: Commonwealth Games 2026: Ramsay-Peaty takes bronze in men's 50m breaststroke final on day four - as it happened
old_text:
Nigeria's Edidiong Umoafia claims the first gold medal of the day, finishing with a score of 319 after lifting 147kg in the snatch and 172kg in the clean and jerk. England's Jonathan Chin has to settle for fourth.
Athletics: Do you, like myself, imagine what poses you'd strike for the camera before your 100m heat? No, just me? OK. After nine heats in the men's 100m, the fastest time belongs to Ghana's Abdul-Rasheed Saminu with 10.01. Two more heats to go.
Swimming: It's the men's 200m butterfly heats, and England's Edward Mildred - who won three relay medals at the 2022 Games - wins the first with a time of 1:57.99. What can Scotland's Duncan Scott offer in the second? Fresh off winning the 200m individual medley, he edges past India's Sajan Prakash to triumph with a time of 1:58.29.
Athletics: A first glimpse of the track at these Games. It's, well, not a gorgeous day in Glasgow. We're taking in the men's 100m, and the third heat belongs to Wales' Jeremiah Azu, bustling to a time of 10.10. He won 60m gold at the world indoor championships last year.
Weightlifting: Over in the men's 71kg final, it's Nigeria's Edidiong Umofia who has taken control of the snatch section, lifting 147kg. England's Jonathan Chin is competing in that final - he's also a full-time doctor who balances 50 to 70-hour weeks with his training.
Here we go again, with 27 gold medals to be won today. It's the start of athletics and para athletics at these Games, and there'll be plenty of focus on the pool with the 50m men's breaststroke final as Adam Ramsay-Peaty tries to execute his "battle plan". The first thing we'll turn to is the men's weightlifting, with medals up for grabs in the 71kg event. There's plenty to get stuck into, and I'll need all the help I can get - drop me a line with your thoughts, hopes, dreams, wishes, whatever you fancy.
new_text:
That, then, is us done for today. It seems a long time ago we started, because it was, which is another way of saying it's been a lot of fun ... and we'll see you again tomorrow. But until then, peace out.
Back with the high jump, Jack of England has one more shot at 2.25 ... and he cant get over. Thus he must settle for bronze, with Kushare and Beckford left to contest the gold.
I can't pretend our men's 110m hurdles final is the highest standard, but it should be a good race; Samuel Bennett of England will fancy himself for gold, but Demario Prince of Jamaica and Milan Trajkovic of Cyprus will have thoughts in that regard too.
We've not been shown anything of the men's high jump final, but Romaine Beckford of Jamaica leads with 2.25m; Sarvesh Kusha of India is second on the same mark, with Kimani Jack of England third on 2.20.
Was Bryce moving wide a plan? I think it may have been because it allowed Sandilands to keep the inside track, and as soon as it happened the race was over.
Ethan Katzberg still leads in the men's hammer with 80.97, hurls his final effort, and it's pretty close to his own mark ... but not quite, I don't think. Still, he's all over this event, a dominant force miles ahead of the competition.
In the 1500m, we've got three Scots, two of whom are Olympic champions - Ben Sandilands won in Paris and Owen Miller in Tokyo. The third of the trio is Steven Bryce, and they train together in Fife; I can't wait to see how things shake out.
Beamish is tailing off! The three Kenyans lead, then Desgagnes of Canada some way behind, with a gap behind him, and it looks like the medals are decided, just not who gets which.
Time for the men's 3000m steeplechase final, with Geordie Beamish of New Zealand, the reigning world champion, looking to become the first non-Kenyan to win since 1982.
Davies says it was a funny race so she tried to stay calm, not do anything silly and be there for the finish. She wasn't expecting to lead from 600m out, but she's glad she did. Tahe last 10m, though, she felt safe, and she's "stoked".
In the men's 800m free final, Sam Short of Australia, the 400m champ, leads by a distance at halfway, with Benjamin Goedemans second and Daniel Wiffen of Northern Ireland third.
Oh man, that's got the eyeballs leaking. We've not a clue what our competitors have invested in making it to here, but we know it's more than we can comprehend.
A tearful Whiston says it's been a very long journey and her dad's just been diagnosed with Parkinson's, so she wanted to make him proud - this race was for him. She didn't see him on the way round, and "sport isn't just about us, it's about the community behind us."
She loves pushing her body to see what it can do and now she wants to cheer on Team England. A school teacher, she thinks her kids will enjoy it and she's really looking forward to watching it back with them.
Davies ran a near-perfect tactical race there, taking advantage of the slow start to kick with plenty in hand, easily taking out Mwangi and driving it home.
